dilemma.author: Apollonius Rhodius
dilemma.locator: Argonautica 3, Medea debates helping Jason; Book 3, normalized characters 42267-44013
dilemma.excerpt: And she thought now that she would give him the charms to cast a spell on the bulls, now that she would not, and that she herself would perish; and again that she would not perish and would not give the charms, but just as she was would endure her fate in silence. Then sitting down she wavered in mind and said: “Poor wretch, must I toss hither and thither in woe? On every side my heart is in despair; nor is there any help for my pain; but it burneth ever thus. Would that I had been slain by the swift shafts of Artemis before I had set eyes on him, before Chalciope’s sons reached the Achaean land. Some god or some Fury brought them hither for our grief, a cause of many tears. Let him perish in the contest if it be his lot to die in the field. For how could I prepare the charms without my parents’ knowledge? What story call I tell them? What trick, what cunning device for aid can I find? If I see him alone, apart from his comrades, shall I greet him? Ill-starred that I am! I cannot hope that I should rest from my sorrows even though he perished; then will evil come to me when he is bereft of life. Perish all shame, perish all glow; may he, saved by my effort, go scatheless wherever his heart desires. But as for me, on the day when he bides the contest in triumph, may I die either straining my neck in the noose from the roof-tree or tasting drugs destructive of life. But even so, when I am dead, they will fling out taunts against me; and every city far away will ring with my doom, and the Colchian women, tossing my name on their lips hither and thither, will revile me with unseemly mocking—the maid who cared so much for a stranger that she died, the maid who disgraced her home and her parents, yielding to a mad passion.

narrativeBlocks.title: Medea's dilemma
narrativeBlocks.body: Medea is Aeetes's daughter, a priestess of Hecate, and the only person in Colchis whose magic can save Jason. Choosing him means betraying her father, her king, and her home — the story makes the choice visible, not inevitable.

narrativeBlocks.title: The charm and the oath
narrativeBlocks.body: In secret she gives Jason a fireproof ointment — smear it on and the bulls' flames cannot touch him — and a plan for the dragon-teeth: throw a stone among the newborn warriors and they will kill each other, mistaking brothers for the thrower.

narrativeBlocks.title: The tasks accomplished
narrativeBlocks.body: Jason yokes the bulls untouched by flame and defeats the earthborn warriors by Medea's trick — the king's murder-proof gauntlet beaten by his own daughter's counsel.

narrativeBlocks.title: The sleepless dragon
narrativeBlocks.body: Aeetes's betrayal makes flight the only option. Medea leads Jason to the grove at night and lulls the guardian dragon to sleep — the fleece is taken, and she flees with the stranger she has bound herself to.

narrativeBlocks.title: Whose feat is it really?
narrativeBlocks.body: Every decisive step — the ointment, the teeth-trick, the dragon — is Medea's. Jason's heroism is real but dependent; the epic quietly asks whether the quest is his triumph or hers.

quiz.prompt: What does Medea give Jason to survive Aeetes's tasks?

choices.text: A magic sword that kills the warriors
A charm that puts Aeetes to sleep
A fireproof ointment against the bulls and a stone-throwing trick to turn the dragon-teeth warriors on each other
Wings to fly past the bulls

quiz.explanation: Medea's magic solves both tasks; without her the quest ends in the field.

quiz.prompt: How is the Golden Fleece finally taken?

choices.text: Jason defeats the dragon in single combat
Aeetes surrenders it after the tasks
The Argonauts seize it in a night raid
Medea lulls its guardian dragon to sleep at night and flees Colchis with Jason

quiz.explanation: The dragon is drugged by Medea; the 'feat' is hers as much as his.
